implementation_notes: In .NET the seam is the interface you own plus a DI registration; the vendor SDK types (`Amazon.S3.IAmazonS3`, `Azure.Storage.Blobs.BlobServiceClient`) are what must stay behind it. `Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection` makes the swap a configuration change, which is exactly the value of the abstraction and exactly the cost if you let SDK types reach the domain models. Two local accelerators of lock-in are worth naming: extension methods on the SDK's types (which spread its idiom through your codebase) and strongly-typed `IConfiguration` binding to the provider's key layout. Audit with the assembly reference graph — every `ProjectReference`/`PackageReference` to a vendor SDK is one strike price.
idiom_name: cloud SDK types in domain models; one extension per provider
pitfalls: Extension methods on vendor types propagate the vendor's design and cannot be removed when it changes.
Binding configuration directly to the provider's key structure (keys named after the service) hard-codes the provider into configuration files.
Strongly-typed clients auto-discover endpoints and credentials, which is convenient and is also an invisible dependency on the provider's configuration model.
